text: A logistics company handles 50,000 shipment exceptions a day. Every exception follows the same four steps: classify the issue, check inventory, calculate a resolution, and notify the customer. The steps rarely change, and cost and latency must be predictable. Which pattern fits best?
options: An autonomous agent that decides the order of the four steps separately for each shipment
A code-driven workflow that runs the four steps in order and calls Claude only where needed
A coordinator agent with four specialist subagents, one for each step
A single Claude call that is given all four tools and the full business rule set
correct_answer: A code-driven workflow that runs the four steps in order and calls Claude only where needed
explanation: If you can draw the flowchart before the first request, you need a workflow, not an agent. A code-driven workflow (B) gives predictable cost and latency and calls Claude only for the steps that need language understanding. An autonomous agent (A) adds cost and variance for a path that never changes. Subagents (C) multiply tokens without a reason such as parallelism or context isolation. One call with every tool (D) hands the fixed sequence to the model instead of enforcing it in code.

text: A support agent drafts refund decisions. Company policy says refunds over $500 always need a manager's approval, with no exceptions. Where should that $500 rule be enforced?
options: In the system prompt, as a clearly worded rule placed at the very top of the instructions
In few-shot examples that show the agent escalating refunds over $500
In an evaluator model that reviews every refund the agent proposes
In deterministic code that checks the amount before the refund tool runs
correct_answer: In deterministic code that checks the amount before the refund tool runs
explanation: Hard financial thresholds that must hold every time belong in deterministic code, such as a gate or PreToolUse hook that checks the amount before the action runs (D). A system prompt (A) and few-shot examples (B) make the right behavior more likely but remain probabilistic. A second model reviewing the refund (C) is also probabilistic, so it cannot guarantee a rule with no exceptions.

text: An architect proposes a coordinator with subagents. Which reason, on its own, justifies a multi-agent design?
options: Researching eight competitors independently, then merging the eight summaries
Making the solution look more sophisticated and advanced to the executive sponsor
Splitting one tightly coupled refactoring task across several agents
Reducing total token cost compared with a single agent
correct_answer: Researching eight competitors independently, then merging the eight summaries
explanation: Multi-agent designs pay off for parallel breadth, context isolation, or separate permissions per role. Eight independent research tasks that merge at the end (A) are a clean example of parallel breadth. Looking advanced (B) is not a technical reason. Tightly coupled work (C) suffers because summaries passed between agents lose shared context. Multi-agent runs usually cost more tokens, not fewer (D), because every worker re-reads its instructions and context.

text: A support assistant costs about $0.17 in tokens per ticket, while each of the 30% of tickets escalated to a human costs $6. Leadership wants to cut the cost per resolved ticket. Which lever usually saves the most?
options: Enabling prompt caching on the shared prompt prefix
Moving every ticket to the smallest and cheapest available model
Raising the AI resolution rate so fewer tickets escalate
Shortening the system prompt to reduce input tokens
correct_answer: Raising the AI resolution rate so fewer tickets escalate
explanation: Optimize the metric the business pays for: here, human escalations ($1.80 per ticket on average) dwarf token cost. Raising the resolution rate (C) saves far more than any token optimization. Prompt caching (A) and a shorter prompt (D) are worth doing but only trim a $0.17 cost. A smaller model (B) may cut tokens but can lower resolution and raise escalations, which costs more.

text: Every night, a compliance team must process 50,000 reports. Results are needed by the next morning, not in real time. Which design choice fits this requirement best?
options: Synchronous Messages API calls, one per report, run in sequence overnight
The Message Batches API, tracking each report with a `custom_id`
An autonomous agent that works through the queue of reports one by one
Streaming responses, so each report starts returning tokens sooner
correct_answer: The Message Batches API, tracking each report with a `custom_id`
explanation: A large overnight job with no real-time need fits the Message Batches API (B): about half the cost of synchronous calls, with `custom_id` to match each result to its report and retry failures. Synchronous calls (A) cost twice as much and compete for rate limits. An agent (C) adds cost and variance to a fixed job. Streaming (D) improves time to first token, which nobody is waiting on here.
